extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging or composing poetic diction — especially the relation of verse to prose, naturalness of language, metre, imagination, and tasteful expression in poetry. Drawn from Coleridge's critical essay on Wordsworth and poetic style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosaic diction (prosaism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines are prosaic when 'the words and the order of the words would find their appropriate place in prose, but are not suitable to metrical composition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with good sense, correct language, and interesting subject-matter, a passage may be justly blamable as prosaic solely because its diction fits prose rather than metre. Examples cited: passages from Daniel's CIVIL WARS. Coleridge warns that many successive lines may be readable as prose and therefore detract from the merit of a poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre must be substantive, not visual
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre should be audible and operative, not merely 'metre to the eye only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge objects to poems whose metre vanishes when transcribed as prose or can be restored by trivial word substitutions (e.g., exchanging final words of rhymed lines). If blank verse can be rendered prose with no change, the metre has become merely visual and the poem's verse-ness is compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural language is not identical with colloquial copying
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's adherence to 'the actual language of men' must not mean slavish transcription of market, wake, high-road, or plough-field speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues the poet should regulate style 'by the principles of grammar, logic, psychology' and by knowledge of material and spiritual facts — in short, by Taste — rather than by directly copying uncultivated speech. Good poetic naturalness arises from informed imagination, not mere imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination/meditation over mere observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The true source of 'genial discrimination' and poetic language is 'the power of imagination proceeding upon the all in each of human nature' — that is, meditation and inward synthesis rather than literal observational copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge contrasts copying words of 'angry or jealous people in uncultivated society' with forming generalized, imaginative expressions. The poet must apprehend human nature and produce characteristic language from inward experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and knowledge govern poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be governed by 'principles of grammar, logic, psychology' and 'a knowledge of the facts, material and spiritual, that most appertain to his art' — together forming Taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge emphasizes that such knowledge, applied by good sense and habit, prevents the poet becoming 'no poet, but a silly or presumptuous usurper.' Taste distinguishes genuine poetic language from fashionable or arbitrary affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical caprices and forced juxtapositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures that force together widely different or incompatible things (e.g., 'the hills are made to reflect the image of a voice') are artificial wit, not true products of fancy or imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such compulsory juxtaposition is 'a species of wit, a pure work of the will' and incompatible with the steady fervour of a mind possessed by its subject. These are to be rejected as mere rhetorical caprice rather than authentic poetic invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine poetic fervour from pseudopoesy
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of 'startling hysteric of weakness' or inflated apostrophes to abstract terms (e.g., Odes to Jealousy, Hope, Oblivion) are pseudopoesy and should be excluded from honours of 'unaffected warmth and elevation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge calls out commonplace magazine odes and over-wrought apostrophes as examples to avoid; true poetic fervour differs qualitatively from such hysterical displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce poetry to external mechanical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If rules were given 'from without' and poetry ceased to be poetry, it would 'sink into a mechanical art.' The rules of the Imagination are powers of growth and production, not external checklists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge warns against attempting to codify poetic diction into rigid formulas; authenticity and instinct are essential, and any externally imposed rule risks morphosis (form without essence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine apt conversational expression with rhyme and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: The rare talent for making 'excellent verses' consists in 'to seek only the apt expression of the thought, and yet to find at the same time with it the rhyme and the metre.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When achieved, this 'neutral style' (common to prose and verse) yields dignified, attractive, and interesting verse that reads like natural speech yet meets metrical demands. Examples: Gellert, Spenser, Chaucer, Herbert, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register must match the emotion: select language by degree of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must distinguish 'the language suitable to suppressed, and the language... characteristic of indulged, anger' and between 'rage and jealousy' — i.e., choose diction appropriate to the kind and intensity of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge asks by what rule a poet is to distinguish these registers, answering that internal imaginative knowledge and taste (not slavish copying) yield the proper language. This is a criterion for authentic characterization and affect in verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial individuality and recognizability
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's diction may be so characteristic that a few lines reveal the author's voice (Coleridge cites Wordsworth and Shakespeare as examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive, individualized diction is a sign of poetic mastery, not a fault. Coleridge uses recognizability as a standard: the 'better half' of a ballad may belong to the poet and be immediately identifiable as his.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of legitimate 'neutral style' across periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'neutral style' — language appropriate to both prose and verse while remaining dignified — exists historically (Chaucer, Spenser, Waller, Herbert) and is not a modern novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge supplies numerous extracts (Chaucer's TROILUS AND CRESEIDE, Herbert's sonnets and poems, Spenser's FAERY QUEEN) to illustrate that natural-sounding diction compatible with metrical form is a recognized excellence and not simply Wordsworthian innovation.
